subject: english-language
title: Cameron and the Myth
welcome_lead: Deborah Cameron dismantles the myth of Mars and Venus. Performance, not essence — gender is what we do.
meta_desc: Deborah Cameron's critique of the difference model and performative gender at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have seen gender re-framed as performance — meta-data, not destiny.

concepts.def: Deborah Cameron (The Myth of Mars and Venus, 2007) showed alleged sex differences are exaggerated and often baseless.
Judith Butler's idea, adopted in linguistics — gender is produced by repeated stylised acts, including talk.
Eckert & McConnell-Ginet's framework, redirecting focus from male/female categories to local practice groups.
Kimberlé Crenshaw's concept — gender intersects with race, class, age and sexuality; language reflects multiple identities at once.
Linguistic features do not directly index gender but index stances and qualities (toughness, care) that are themselves gendered.
Awareness of gender stereotypes can shape speakers' own performance, reinforcing supposed differences.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Cameron reviewed meta-analyses and found tiny or no average differences between men and women in talkativeness, interruption and politeness.

Popular self-help books, she argued, exploited and amplified stereotypes that did not survive scrutiny.

Butler frames gender as performative: identity is produced through repeated stylised acts. Choice of address terms, intonation patterns and discourse markers helps perform a gendered self in context.

This shifts the question from do women speak differently? to how is gender being done here?

Crenshaw reminds us that gender does not act alone. A young Black woman in MLE-speaking London performs gender, race, age and locale simultaneously.

Modern sociolinguistic gender research takes intersectionality as a starting point, not an add-on.

mcqs.q: Are claims that women use more 'tentative' language well-supported?
options: Chomsky said children should be taught grammar from age two.
Women and men have different vocal cords so speak differently.
Women always use more hedges and tag questions than men.
Early studies (Lakoff) made broad claims, but later research (e.g. Holmes, Cameron) shows context matters more than gender, and many supposed differences disappear with proper data.

options: Skinner believed children couldn't learn language until age five.
